result.summary: This section gathers three testimonia about a lost epic, the Story of Oedipus (Oedipodea). They record its length and attribution to Cinaethon, its claim that Oedipus's sons were born of Euryganeia rather than Iocasta, and a line saying the Sphinx killed Haemon, son of Creon.

scenes.title: Fragments of a lost epic
scenes.summary: Three ancient citations describe the Story of Oedipus: its author and length, the mother of Oedipus's sons, and the Sphinx's killing of Haemon.

notable_quotes.reason: Preserves a variant tradition denying that Oedipus fathered children with his mother Iocasta.

analysis.text: The fragments show that the Oedipus myth had variants, including one that avoided children born of incest.
The epic is lost, known only through quotations by Pausanias and scholiasts, showing how much early Greek epic survives only in scraps.

legacy.text: The Theban cycle of epics, including the Oedipodea, fed the tragedians, notably Sophocles and Euripides, who reshaped the myth.

fun_facts.text: The inscription cited credits the epic with 6,600 lines, a length given by an ancient record.

language_notes.text: 'Verses' means lines of epic poetry; 6,600 lines gives the poem's length, roughly half an Iliad's size.
'Judging by Homer' refers to the Odyssey, where Epicaste (Iocasta) is Oedipus's mother and wife but no children by her are mentioned.
A scholiast is an ancient commentator whose notes were copied in the margins of a text, here Euripides' Phoenician Women.

context_notes.text: Cinaethon of Sparta was a poet credited with several early epics. This inscription is a catalogue entry, not the poem itself.
Pausanias was a 2nd-century AD Greek traveller whose guidebook to Greece often records local myths and variant versions.
Haemon, son of Creon, is best known as Antigone's betrothed in Sophocles. Here a different tradition has the Sphinx kill him.

literary_notes.text: 'Noble,' 'blameless' and 'dear' are formulaic descriptors typical of epic style, praising Haemon and Creon.
Stressing the boy's beauty and loveliness makes his death at the Sphinx's hands more poignant.
